runtime: # conformance.tsv — the invalid-half conformance counts, for BOTH runtimes,
# in ONE file.
# Read by ts/test/toml.test.ts and go/toml_valid_test.go through the shared
# @tabnas/support loader, so neither can read it differently from the other.
#   runtime    ts | go
#   total      how many documents the suite must have found
#   rejected   how many the port refuses
#   diagnosed  how many of those refusals are real parse errors
#   crashes    rejections that are really internal crashes (rejected minus
#              diagnosed); a rejection that is a crash is not conformance
# WHY THIS FILE EXISTS
# These numbers used to live twice, as INVALID_FLOOR / INVALID_DIAGNOSED_FLOOR
# in the TypeScript suite and invalidFloor / invalidDiagnosedFloor in the Go
# one. Both were commented "MEASURED on 2026-08-09" against this same pinned
# corpus. They read 227/212 and 230/230. Nothing compared them, and nothing
# ever would have: they were in different files, in different languages, in
# different test frameworks.
# WHY THEY ARE EXACT, NOT FLOORS
# A floor is a lower bound, so it absorbs degradation silently. The TypeScript
# diagnosed floor sat 11 below its own measured value, which meant eleven
# documents could have decayed from a diagnosed error into an internal crash
# with the build still green. That is precisely the failure the 2026-08 fleet
# audit was written about, sitting inside the instrument meant to catch it.
# The corpus is pinned by commit (see scripts/fetch-toml-test.sh), so the
# counts are deterministic and an exact match is the honest assertion. Movement
# in EITHER direction is now a failing build:
#   went up   the grammar improved. Re-measure and update this file. Good news
#             that still has to be written down.
#   went down something regressed. Do not edit this file to make it pass.
# THE GAP BETWEEN THE ts AND go ROWS IS REAL AND IS NOT A ROUNDING ERROR
# go rejects 2 more documents than ts: string/bad-uni-esc-07 and
# string/bad-uni-esc-ml-07, the `\u12g4` escape. TypeScript reads a
# hexadecimal escape laxly and accepts both; Go's scan is strict and
# rejects with invalid_unicode. That is the "lax hexadecimal scan" row of
# ../test/divergent.tsv, where Go is the repair TARGET and the two that
# move are TypeScript and Rust, so this gap closes from the ts side.
# WHY EVERY ROW WENT UP AGAIN, ts 309 -> 316, go 311 -> 318, rust 309 ->
# The seven are a key a table already holds from an EARLIER header. A
# table's body is parsed into a map of its own and merged into the table
# when the body ends, so the checks below, which read the body's map, never
# saw the table's own keys, and the merge replaced them: `[a.b]` `c = 1`
# then `[a]` `b = 2` gave {"a":{"b":2}}, losing `c`; `[a.b.c]` `z = 9` then
# `[a]` `b.c.t = 1` lost `z`; `[[a.b]]` then `[a]` `b.y = 2` replaced the
# array. Every port now checks a key at the top of a table body against the
# table as well, where the body defines it (bodyTable in ts/src/toml.ts and
# go/refs.go, body_conflict in rs/src/refs.rs), and refuses it with
# toml_key_conflict at the key. Obtained by diffing the accepted sets before
# and after, in each port; the same seven in all three, and no other
# document changed its answer:
#   array/extend-defined-aot  inline-table/overwrite-09
#   table/append-with-dotted-keys-01  table/append-with-dotted-keys-02
#   table/append-with-dotted-keys-03  table/append-with-dotted-keys-08
#   table/overwrite-array-in-parent
# The valid half does not move: 268 of 268 in every port, before and after.
# What stays accepted in this family, and why: an inline table or an array
# written as a value is not yet closed to a later header or dotted key
# reaching INTO it (`a = {}` then `[a.b]`, `a = [1]` then `a.b = 2`;
# inline-table/duplicate-key-03, overwrite-02, overwrite-07, overwrite-08,
# spec-1.1.0/common-49-0, array/extending-table, array/tables-01,
# table/duplicate-key-10). inline-table/overwrite-01 is refused, but with
# `unexpected`: a plain key after a dotted key at the top of a document or
# a body is a grammar limit of its own (tabnas/toml#94).
# WHY EVERY ROW WENT UP, ts 278 -> 309, go 280 -> 311, rust 278 -> 309,
# The thirty-one are four shapes TOML forbids and every port accepted,
# building a value TOML says does not exist: a key given a second value
# (`a = 1` then `a = 2`, which the base grammar's duplicate-key rule read
# as last wins, and `tbl = {k = 1}` then `tbl = {kk = 2}`, which it
# merged), the same inside an inline table (`a = {b = 1, b = 2}`), a
# header written twice (`[a]` then `[a]`), and a header for a table a
# dotted key or an inline table had already defined (`a.b = 1` then `[a]`,
# `a = {}` then `[a]`). All three ports refuse them with toml_key_conflict
# since the same change (ts/src/toml.ts, go/refs.go, rs/src/node.rs and
# rs/src/refs.rs): a pair or a dotted key's last segment refuses a key the
# table already holds, and a header may define an existing table only when
# its own prefix created it and no header has defined it yet. Obtained by
# diffing the accepted sets before and after, in each port; the same
# thirty-one in all three:
#   inline-table/duplicate-key-01  inline-table/duplicate-key-02
#   inline-table/overwrite-03  inline-table/overwrite-05
#   key/duplicate-keys-01 .. key/duplicate-keys-09 (nine)
#   spec-1.0.0/table-9-0  spec-1.0.0/table-9-1
#   spec-1.1.0/common-46-0  spec-1.1.0/common-46-1
#   table/append-with-dotted-keys-04  table/append-with-dotted-keys-05
#   table/duplicate-key-01  table/duplicate-key-04  table/duplicate-key-05
#   table/duplicate-key-08  table/duplicate-key-09  table/duplicate-key-11
#   table/duplicate-key-12  table/duplicate-key-13  table/duplicate-key-14
#   table/redefine-02  table/redefine-03  table/super-twice
# The valid half does not move: 268 of 268 in every port, before and after.
# What that change left accepted in this family: a key the table already
# held from an EARLIER header, overwritten when the table's body was merged
# (refused since, above), and an inline table not yet closed to a later
# header or dotted key reaching INTO it. Neither was among the four shapes.
# The nineteen are the key-conflict class (audit items T4 and T5): a key
# redefined as a table or a table-array header, an array of tables
# redefined as a table, a dotted key through a value. TypeScript and Rust
# diagnosed them with toml_key_conflict; Go accepted every one and lost data
# doing it, and this file used to say it could not do otherwise, because
# its engine converted every panic raised inside a grammar action into an
# `internal` error. The engine has since passed a *TabnasError panic through
# with its code intact (tabnas/parser go/parser.go, startParse), so the Go
# port now raises the code where the other two do (go/refs.go, tableAt and
# arrayAt). Obtained by diffing the accepted sets of the two ports, not by
# subtracting totals:
#   array/tables-02  inline-table/duplicate-key-04  inline-table/overwrite-04
#   inline-table/overwrite-06  inline-table/overwrite-10
#   key/dotted-redefine-table-01  key/dotted-redefine-table-02
#   table/append-with-dotted-keys-06  table/append-with-dotted-keys-07
#   table/array-implicit  table/duplicate-key-02  table/duplicate-key-03
#   table/duplicate-key-06  table/duplicate-key-07  table/newline-04
#   table/overwrite-bool-with-array  table/overwrite-with-deep-table
#   table/redefine-01  table/trailing-dot
# TypeScript rejects a twentieth with this code, table/array-empty, which Go
# already refused with another one, so it moves no number.
# WHY go WENT DOWN, AND WHY THAT IS NOT A REGRESSION
# go 269 -> 261 on 2026-08-20. "Went down: do not edit this file to make it
# pass" is the right default and this is the documented exception, so the
# evidence is here rather than in a commit message.
# The delta is exactly eight documents, obtained by diffing the rejected sets
# from the two builds rather than subtracting the totals:
#   string/no-open-01..08.toml     s = a"   a = [a"]   a = a"""   a = [a''']
# Nothing was gained back, and nothing else moved. Every one is the shape of
# parser audit item P1 (tabnas/parser#128): unquoted text followed by a quote.
# The Go engine's text matcher used to END a text run at a string-quote
# character, which TypeScript's never did, so these eight were refused by the
# STRING matcher — `unprintable` for the single-quote cases,
# `unterminated_string` for the triple-quote ones. That refusal was the defect,
# not a conformance check: TypeScript rejects NONE of the eight and never did.
# So the number falls because an accidental rejection stopped happening, and
# the two ports now agree on all eight.
# What this does NOT fix: `s = a"` is invalid TOML — a bare unquoted value is
# not legal at all — and both ports now accept it. No engine change can help;
# it is this grammar accepting a bare value where the spec allows none. New
# register item. "We align with TypeScript" and "we are correct" are different
# claims, and this is where they come apart.
# MEASURE AGAINST THE SIBLING CHECKOUTS, NOT THE PINNED RELEASE
# The shared polyglot-ci workflow clones each tabnas dependency and wires a
# `go work use` / npm symlink over it, so these suites run against parser's
# `main` — NOT the release that go/go.mod and ts/package.json pin. A number
# taken against the published pin is for a build the gate never runs, on
# the days the two builds agree (2026-10-02, below) as on the days they do
# not (while the pin was v0.8.10, it gave go=234). Use admin/scripts/link.sh
# (or a go.work over the siblings) before re-measuring, and write down what
# the numbers were measured against.
# THE rust ROW REPRODUCES THE ts ROW, WHICH IS THE POINT
# The Rust port measures 316/316/0, the same three numbers as TypeScript, on
# the same corpus. It diagnoses the key-conflict class as TypeScript does,
# and reads the `\u12g4` escape laxly as TypeScript does, so it sits on the
# ts side of the two-document gap above.
# One thing it does differently, and it changes no number. The
# encoding/bad-utf8-* documents are not valid UTF-8 and a Rust string cannot
# hold them, so the suite decodes them lossily and the parser sees U+FFFD.
# That is what Node hands the TypeScript suite as well; Go is the odd one
# out, because a Go string holds arbitrary bytes. All three rows count the
# same outcome for those documents either way.
